content: Lomatium is a genus consisting of 70 to 80 species of perennial herbs that are native to the western regions of North America. Among these species, Lomatium cous, Lomatium geyeri, and Lomatium macrocarpum are commonly referred to as biscuit roots due to their starchy, edible roots. These roots have historically served as traditional foods for Native American communities. They were consumed either cooked or dried and subsequently ground into flour. The flavor of these roots has been described as resembling celery, parsnip, or even stale biscuits. Certain species within this genus, such as Lomatium dissectum, have been utilized in herbal medicine, particularly for the treatment of coughs and upper respiratory infections. Research conducted by the University of British Columbia has demonstrated that extracts derived from Lomatium dissectum possess the ability to immobilize Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium in laboratory settings. However, the effectiveness of these extracts in human subjects has not yet been evaluated. It is important to note that this plant family is also recognized for including members that are highly toxic.
